utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Mr. Harvey, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Nina Mileva, who is just behind the pillar here, who has been with my team for the last six months, is from Skopje, Macedonia, and is studying at the University of Amsterdam and is a very impressive linguist assisting us on our B/C/S translations and work. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. McKenna, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 25 of your statement you said that: "I can say with a high degree of certainty that during that period of chaos, the local Serbian leadership had almost no contact with the leadership at Pale." However, in your Grujic testimony, you said that you weren't sure what sort of road communications existed between Zvornik and Pale between April and July of that year. Do you stand by that testimony today, that you weren't sure what type of road communications there were during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes, Mr. Karadzic? Objection?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is a linguistic matter. What was said in Belgrade is the same as what this witness said. He didn't say, "I'm not sure whether there were any," but he said, "I'm not sure that there were any." Now, in the question the meaning was shifted. It may be best to show him the text from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Certainly. Could we have 65 ter number 25093.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And this, Mr. Ivanovic, is the text from your testimony in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And I'd like to see page 37 of the English and page 26 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, the discussion - and this is at the bottom of the page in the English version - is you're asked by the Presiding Judge: "Was it possible -- were there roads that could go to Pale prior to Karisik arriving?" And you say: "I don't know -- in the first days, everyone was focusing on themselves." And you're asked: "Not in the first days, later on, in May and June," I think we need to turn to the next page, and you said, "they're all early days. Well, I don't know what road communications were like. I'm not sure. I'm not quite sure." And then further on you say: "Again, I don't know. I don't know what sort of road communications there were."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we see the Serbian? Could we see the Serbian page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I believe it's page 26 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, have you had a chance to review your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kindly ask for the relevant page to be displayed, the page in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, did you read the part, relevant part, from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did sometime before, but I don't really know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's show the part. I cannot help you, Mr. Karadzic, here, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Karadzic could direct us to the correct part. I believe it's on page 26.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that answer is not on this page. I either need a hard copy or we must display the different pages. Perhaps we can print out a couple of pages. I think it may be page 25. Could we get the previous page back. Oh, yes, it's at the top of the page. The answer to the previous question must be the first one on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Then could you put your question again, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: If you've had a chance to review your testimony, I'll ask you whether you stand by your testimony in the Grujic case that you don't know what type of road communications there were in the period between -- sorry, road communications there were between Zvornik and Pale in the period between April and July 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and now I can confirm that I don't know exactly what kind of road communications there were, but during the first months, I never, ever went to Pale because I wasn't sure I'd be safe.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the previous page, page 24?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you can take up this issue in your re-examination. Let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And yesterday, as you explained, after you were beaten up, you didn't participate in -- in fact, you shied away from the municipality, the army, and the paramilitaries, and that was at T 39868. So, Mr. Ivanovic, you're not really in a position to testify about the communications or the contact that the local Serbian leadership had with the Pale leadership following the breakout of the war, are you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear the interpretation of this last bit well, but you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Then I will ask Ms. McKenna to repeat her question, in particular the last part.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, do you agree that you are not in a position to testify about the contact that the local Serbian leadership had with the Pale leadership following the breakout of the war?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can speak about that. I was not in the ranks of the authorities. I was a man of the economy. I had some contacts with people, but not on the basis of political power.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note that I'm coming to the end of my time. I will ask for perhaps 15 minutes. I understand that it's in excess of what I was given, but I would like to cover some additional topics that are relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In paragraph 28 you -- of your statement, you say that it was only after the paramilitaries had been arrested at the end of July that many of the crimes committed by these paramilitaries were discovered. Now, I'd like to talk about the awareness of crime being committed that you spoke about in your previous statements and in your testimony in the Grujic case. And again I'd like you to focus on the questions I'm asking, keep your answers short, and answer yes or no where possible. These are all matters that you've previously testified about or given a statement about. Firstly I'd like to talk about the Karakaj technical school. Mr. Ivanovic, you knew at the time that there were detentions at the Karakaj technical school, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time? You said "at the time," but I'm not sure which time you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: You knew during the period between April and July 1992, so prior to the paramilitaries being discovered or being arrested, you knew that there were detentions at Karakaj technical school?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard something about that, but nothing specific, nothing certain. But people talked, the people I worked with at the factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, you heard or you knew that the detainees included men from Djulici, some former employees of your factory, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you heard of the killings that took place at Karakaj technical school two or three days after they occurred, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I heard of them but with what delay, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, do you accept that it was in -- a matter of a number of days that you heard about them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see again Mr. Ivanovic's testimony in the Grujic case, and this time I'd like to look at page 23 of the English and page 16 to 17 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ivanovic, with reference to the villagers from Djulici you said: "It is known that men were taken to the school, to the high school in Karakaj, while women and children went to Tuzla, I guess." And you were asked: "When did you hear this, after how many days did you hear this?" And you said: "Well, I do not know exactly, but it was during this period. Was it two or three days after those events, I do not know." And your -- and you're asked when they were killed and then you heard about it, and you said: "Correct." And you said: "This was simply the word on the street. People spoke only about that." So do you accept, as you testified previously, that shortly after the killings took place you heard of them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The questions are much like the ones you're asking me now. I said I didn't know a couple of days, two, three days, thereabouts, and my answers now are the same as they were then. Yeah, I'm not sure how many days elapsed, two, three, five, but it was those days immediately after the events.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And people were saying that 700 to 800 men were held there and killed there. Isn't that what they were saying at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody mentioned exact numbers then. Nobody mentioned 700 to 800 people. Only later on I learned from the media about the number of people and that's how I came up with that number. Nobody knew how many people had been killed in that period of time. It's all hearsay. I don't really have real information about it. I never went near that school. I steered clear of all these crimes. I was afraid of that. That's nothing for normal people. These are abnormal things. I don't know how to explain that to you. I said already God forbid that you find yourself in such circumstances because only then would you really understand. There was a war and things were far from normal. They were out of control, especially in such a religious and ethnic war as went on there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic. Again, I'm going to ask you to focus quite specifically on the questions and -- but -- and I'd like to focus on just what your knowledge was or what you heard at the time. Let's talk about Celopek Dom Kulture. Again, you heard at the time about the detentions in Celopek Dom Kulture, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you heard that the detainees were from Divici, from Djulici, and from Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really sure that I knew they were from Djulici because I think the word was that those from Djulici were being detained at Karakaj, whereas at Celopek there were people from Divici. That's my memory now anyway. I don't quite remember what exactly I said before. There may have been people from Djulici, though. I can't remember exactly. I don't know that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that some people were there. I was passing by that place. Some guys were keeping guard. I never saw the detainees themselves, though, they were inside. But it was on the way -- on my way to work and back and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: But you heard at the time about the mistreatment and killings that were taking place there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard some stories. There was talk about some bad guys going in there, beating people up, mistreating them. I don't know, possibly even killing people, but nothing specific. Yeah, people talked.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And people also talked about the fact that there were killings in Gero's slaughter-house, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that later, but not while that was going on. You can believe me that even today I don't know where that slaughter-house is. It isn't a place I know. But later, at a later time, I heard of that slaughter-house too. It's a slaughter-house where during the Second World War many Serbs were killed and this was some sort of vengeance. I don't know much about that slaughter-house, though, but as I said, later on I heard that there was some killings there although nothing specific.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like to move now to your knowledge of the events in July 1995. At paragraph 31 of your statement you talked about the fighting that was occurring in the Zvornik municipality and you say you heard that a large number of Muslim soldiers had died in the fighting. Now, in your previous interview with the OTP on the 13th of October, 2000, which was recorded on tape, you gave more details about what you heard at the time in relation to Muslims being killed in your area. So I'm going to ask you to confirm some of these details. So is it correct that you heard stories about buses of people being brought through villages in your area with their hands behind their neck and directed to schools in Rocevic and Pilica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard stories. Sometimes I even saw some buses that were going to Batkovici. Some people said that some were in Bijeljina municipality, a place I never saw, and that they were taking these detainees there. I don't know where they had come from. And as for schools and detainees, yeah, people talked, where I lived in my village, that Muslims were being taken there and that there had been some killings. Yes, there were stories about that and I heard those stories.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you heard that the people taken to those schools were taken and killed, as you've said, for instance, in gravel pits, in Kozluk, and in Pilica school itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure at the school at Pilica itself. From what I heard, the people weren't killed there but taken to some Dom Kulture as it was called, but it wasn't really that. It was more of a co-op facility, as the communists had built earlier for agricultural co-operatives and that place up there was a school, I don't remember exactly which place you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm just going to read a passage from your previous testimony to refresh your memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And for the parties' reference this is 65 ter 25214, page 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And you said: "I lived through -- I lived through those two hard months. I heard terrible stories about killings. These stories were circulating at the time. That there were some killings committed in school in Pilica, some people killed on those pit holes, pits by the Drina River, that's what I heard. It was a secret when those bodies were buried, because it became the subject of interest for all various kinds of international organisations." Does that refresh your memory as to what you heard about the killings at the school in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the time I thought it was at the school, but it wasn't really. It was at the co-operative building and that's what I learned later. But it's not a big difference, the distance between the two was a kilometre or two. They weren't really at the school there, or rather, they were but for a short period of time and then they were moved to that co-operative building because the school is probably too small, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that the killings that happened in your area, in and around your village, in Kozluk and in Pilica, were public knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The killings didn't take place in my village but in another, but doesn't matter. I understand. Public knowledge, I don't know [as interpreted], but the people who lived near to these places simply saw what was going on and that how stories spread. You can't hide anything from the Serbian people. The Serbs speak about all sorts of things, what they're supposed to talk about and what not. And after a couple of years you can certainly learn the truth from the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't correctly recorded in line 23. [In English] "I understand. Public knowledge, I don't know." [Interpretation] He didn't say he didn't know but he said it was not public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, even now I said it was not public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. At the end of your answer, Mr. Ivanovic, you said this, I quote: "You can't hide anything from the Serbian people. The Serbs speak about all sorts of things, what they are supposed to talk about and what not. And after a couple of years, you can certainly learn the truth from the Serbian people." I don't follow what they are supposed to talk about and what not. Could you expand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if two Serbs quarrel, then rest assured that they will try to lie. One will try to lie about the other one. Yesterday there was a question put by the Prosecutor as to what I stated about Brano Grujic, when it was mentioned in the newspapers, Sky News, et cetera. At that moment we were not on good terms so there was sort of a bit of teasing involved, so I tried to take "revenge," and that's why I said yesterday, okay, I apologise to Brano Grujic, I haven't read that, I haven't heard that. I don't know whether you understand that now. You know what you asked me now about Srebrenica, you know what, what was crystallised there was this story about Srebrenica, that one -- I don't know. There was a number of people who had surrendered and who were locked up in these facilities and a very large number who had not surrendered and who went on towards Muslim-held territory and who were fighting along the way. And in that fighting, if that's what you're asking me, a lot of people got killed, a lot of Muslims got killed, a lot of Serbs got killed too, especially young men from my village. There were many casualties and one day there were three funerals. So that's the assumption. That's what I heard, that had everybody surrendered, nobody would have been killed. But in this fighting, a lot of Serbs got killed and then some bad guys from the Serb side took their revenge against these people. The Serb people never did that in history. The Serb people are a freedom-loving people and that is something that the Serbs there want the most, that this Tribunal or world justice establish -- oh, I am sorry. We, the local Serb population there and the Serb people in Republika Srpska in general, we would want it to be established who it was that committed these killings. If I spoke fast, the Serb people in Republika Srpska and the Serb people in general are a freedom-loving people and in history they never committed any crimes, and that is why we care about it being established what actually happened during those days after the fall of Srebrenica. Just another thing, if I may say something as a member of the Serb people. I would like to ask this Tribunal to shed light on the killing of Serb civilians in Sarajevo. They were killed there and tortured and the number of fatalities the same like Muslims in Srebrenica, and Serbs are bitter because nobody was prosecuted for that, for what happened in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, I'm not sure if I followed you in full when you said, "If two Serbs quarrel, they will try to lie." So with respect to Srebrenica, what is lie and what is truth? Could you clarify, Mr. Ivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, look, perhaps you did not understand me very well then. I wasn't talking about any kind of lies. I mean, what I found out, that is to say, I was not there directly, I heard about all of this, but over all these years, if it is important what these people there are saying -- I mean I cannot talk about things that people are talking about that I hadn't heard of. I can only talk about what I heard of. It's what I said. A certain number surrendered and part of these people lost their lives, how many I don't know. But a considerable number did not surrender. They were fighting. They continued fighting, lots of them lost their lives, lots of Serbs lost their lives, and then when these others got killed and then their nearest and dearest also got killed, then they took revenge against those who had been detained. Let me not repeat this, this is inappropriate, but it did happen. Who did this and why? Again, I can just convey what I've already said. The man that you are trying here, our president, Mr. Karadzic, did not do that. That is 101 per cent certain. I have a technical education. You cannot say that. You can always say 100 per cent sure. So we are 100 per cent sure. He did not order that. We know all the efforts that he made, everything that he did, et cetera. So this happened. It would be a good thing, not only for Mr. Karadzic, but for all of us in Republika Srpska to establish exactly who it was that ordered this and so on. Even these international conspiracies are mentioned and so on. I don't know what the truth is. I saw these documentaries coming from here, from the West, and they refer to these international interferences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Back to you, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I have one very brief topic for which I would like to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in private session, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, as we've seen, the account of events that you gave in your statement to the Defence differs in some significant aspects from the statements that you've given previously to the Office of the Prosecutor. Now, after you spoke to the Prosecution previously, rumours spread in Zvornik that you had spoken to them and you had given away --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. But what's the reason for the private session?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It will become apparent, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: After you'd spoken to the Prosecution previously, rumours spread in Zvornik that you had spoken to them and given away some information about some people that you were not supposed to. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is absolutely not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 25117.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, this is your statement of March 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And I'm interested in page 11 of the English and page 16 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: And in the final paragraph of your statement you say: "For the time being I'm not willing to testify because of my family and my security concerns, but ICTY can use my statement as evidence. After I spoke to ICTY investigators last year, the rumours spread in town that I talked to the investigators and gave away some information about some people that I was not supposed to." So can you confirm that that is what you stated to the investigators? You will see your initials on that page.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that but I have to explain why I said that. I had some conflicts with some policemen there on the Drina, they were Mafia, not police. I know that now; I didn't know it then. I was afraid of those people. It was in that context. So it's not in the context of what you were asking about roughly or what you were intimating.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In Ivanovic, I put it to you that it's in your interest to testify publicly now, giving an account of events that is favourable to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but I don't know what you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether it will assist your position to be seen to be testifying publicly, giving an account of events that is favourable to the Defence in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely. I never asked for protection. Whenever I testified, I always speak publicly. I was never afraid, ever, in my life of what I state. I said last time too. For five or six hours these investigators who were putting questions to me, they're so boring, they keep asking you things and then I say five times that I don't know something and then the sixth time I probably say something I'm not supposed to say. I'm a technologist, I'm not a lawyer. And then you -- well, for the most part I simply couldn't read this anymore and I just sign it because then you have to spend another three hours reading all of it. You know, I never could take that kind of thing. I couldn't take lawyers. I don't like this system of work and so on. I like being efficient, practical. That's it. I have no reason to hide anything or I don't need any kind of protection. As far as I'm concerned, you don't have to draw any kind of blinds or curtains or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I still don't follow why we had to be in private session. The statement is in public?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: That's true. I'm sorry, Your Honour. It was out of an abundance of caution for the security of the witness, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we go -- and so Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: We would have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ivanovic, you have no difficulty with lifting the confidentiality of the conversation that you just had with the Prosecutor? Put otherwise, do you have any problem with making public your previous conversation with the -- with Ms. McKenna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be accessible to the public. Everything I said should be made accessible to the public, everything I said yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We go back to open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. McKenna. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, let us remember to pause between questions and answers, and I'll start with the things that you said just now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please call up P6403. Could we please have that in e-court, P, Prosecution number, 6403. And then could I have page 16, or rather, 17. 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Ivanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 16 in the text or 17 -- no, this is the 16. Well, now the next one -- just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: About 100 persons, et cetera, that's what is here. You were asked whether people knew or did not know, whether this was accessible to the public --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please wait until we have the relevant English page as well. Do you have the page number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately, but it was called up by Ms. McKenna. Page 16 in Serbian and right after that page 17. I think it's 24 in English. Yes, that's it. Now could we have the next page in both languages, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, this is what I'm interested in. Could you read your second answer from the top, "Let me tell you ..." et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. "Well, let me tell you, these things were not done EPP or publicly. I assume all of that was done in some secret way, that is to say, really, when this happened, nobody knew about it." That is probably concerning those killings for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Before time passes by. For record I hereby confirm again that the audio/video part and the transcript of the private session should be lifted, to be public. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what EPP means?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, literally it stands for economic propaganda programme. Let me just read this once again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Commercials on television.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was not done publicly. You know, it's not that somebody was bragging about that. Well, you know, EPP, when you really want everybody to know about something, you know, marketing and things, then I said I assumed that all of this was done in some secret way and that no one knew about that, how it happened, where it happened, and so on, except for these people who actually did it, of course. Like any secret operation, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that your position today as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us look at page 24. You were asked about whether you knew that there were no communications and whether you knew or did not know about the existence of communications. This is a bit complicated, so let us take a look at page 24 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 24 in Serbian, the next page in Serbian. The bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge is asking you about these policemen, who commanded them in Zvornik, these policemen. Do you see that towards the bottom?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Page 37 in English. And he's asking you who commanded these policemen and you say possibly this Pantelic and so on. Then the Presiding Judge says: "Is there anyone above him there?" And you say: "Believe me, I don't know. There was no one, I think. I might be wrong, but at the time there was no -- further on towards, I don't know, Pale or" -- And the President of the Chamber says: "There wasn't?" And you say: "I think there wasn't. I don't know when Karisik's police came to Zvornik, but when that police came to Zvornik, then some sort of order was actually installed ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object at this point. I'm not clear how the issue of who was in command of the policemen in Zvornik arose from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Ivanovic is answering here that he did not know whether there was any communication towards Pale, he doesn't know of its existence, and that is a question of linguistic nuance. And that was raised in the cross-examination. As a matter of fact, this page was called up, 23, 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, but this is not related to you as such. But how the current question is related to the communication thing?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in the cross-examination the question was raised, and this page was even called up, as if Mr. Ivanovic had said that he had not known whether there had been communication or not. And I'm saying this is a question of linguistic nuance. He said, "I didn't know that it existed. I don't think there was any but I may be mistaken," it's page 5, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But what -- but your question related to who, as to who commanded these policemen. How is that question related to the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, please take a look at what the President of the Chamber is asking him, whether there was someone above them, above these local commanders. And then it gets to this question of whether there was any communication with the centre. I see here, Presiding Judge: "And is there anyone above him there?" And then Mr. Ivanovic says that: "Maybe I'm" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find the passage first. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Last third, or rather, from the middle of the page. [In English] "Presiding Judge: And who commanded him? Is there anyone there above him?" Witness Jovan Ivanovic: "Believe me there was no one. I believe I might be wrong but at that time there was none" -- oh, my God. This is -- [Interpretation] This is a mistranslation, a total mistranslation in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, but how is that question arising from the issue of communication? Where does that -- the communication issue appear, Ms. McKenna, what page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: The communication issue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this on this page?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's on this page but the question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: It's at the very bottom. Mr. Ivanovic was asked: "Was it possible -- were there roads that could go to this Pale place prior to Karisik arriving?" And it continues, the discussion continues about the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: I would also, while I'm on my feet, object to Mr. Karadzic reading tracts of the witness's previous evidence to him, as that is clearly leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please move on to another topic. The Chamber agrees with Ms. McKenna's observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I might be missing something but -- or maybe the Chamber's missing something, and it's difficult when we don't know the language what Dr. Karadzic is trying to convey to us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm fine with him dealing with the language issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's what he's been dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: To come back to that issue, not this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's unfortunate this part was mixed with the part communication towards Pale. This business about commanding was -- the context was presented in connection with communication towards Pale --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. You can explain to us in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's better if Dr. Karadzic just goes on and asks him another question, but if you give him the latitude to explore this, I think he would be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, if you could excuse yourself for some moments.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just talking about the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karadzic, you can explain how these issues are interrelated and ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, Ms. McKenna called up this page to prove that, at some point in time, Mr. Ivanovic made a different statement in terms of communication between Zvornik and Pale. The translation into English is completely wrong. He did not say "there was no one." He said "there was none." [In English] Concerning the communication. [Interpretation] And it's linked to this. The Presiding Judge there is asking who was above them? The one above them is in Pale and that is how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, let's go on. Where did he say "there is none"?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where it is. The Presiding Judge says: "And is there anyone above him there?" And then his answer that follows that and then he says there was -- [In English] "There was no one." "There didn't exist" should be translated, that "there didn't exist." "I think I may be wrong, but in that time there was no existing any further" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, just a second --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: -- towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I found that location. But it reads like this: "And who commands him? Is there anyone there above him? "I don't know. Believe me. There was no one. I believe I might be wrong but at the time there was none." But how is this passage related to the communication issue which Ms. McKenna raised?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because whoever would be above this local police would be in Pale, and he didn't say "there was no one." He used the feminine "it did not exist," meaning there was no communication. Because this one who would be above would have to be in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't follow. You're saying that he didn't say "there was no one," what do you mean? He said "there was no one," but you say he didn't say "there was no one."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, "nije postojala," that means that something that is in the feminine had not existed. And the translation there says "there was no one," "there was nobody." And that's not true. And then he says: "I don't think it existed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the question for that answer? "Who commands him? Is there anyone there above him?" That was the question. And according to you then, the answer was: "It didn't exist." So it means that there was no one who commanded him. I don't know what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no, towards Pale. There was no towards Pale, towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. So could you read out the Serbian passage slowly. Where is it in the B/C/S part?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last third.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if you could read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presiding Judge says: "All right. Who commands them? "Ivanovic: Who, the police? "The Presiding Judge: These policemen, that senior cadre in Zvornik. "Ivanovic: It is possible that that Pantelic person was it then." "Presiding Judge: And who commands him, is there anyone there above him?" "Ivanovic: Believe me, I don't know. It did not exist, I think. I might be wrong, but there at that time there was no -- further on, towards, I don't know, Pale or ..." "Presiding Judge: There wasn't?" "Ivanovic: I think it didn't exist ..." and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I see a translation issue here. The Chamber finds it may be related to the method of communication at the time. We'll allow the question to be continued. Shall we bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, where should we begin again. What is your question for the witness, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to ask the witness to read the second-last answer and to tell us what it was that did not exist towards Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the gist of the answer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand the question. The gist of this answer is that there was no -- in the days of chaos and when the paramilitaries were engaging in atrocities, realistically speaking there could be no co-ordination with the leadership in Pale. First and foremost, I have in mind Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and their closest associates. There was no electronic communication, the lines were down. We did have some connection with Serbia locally, but Bosnia as a whole did not, and the roads were as they were. So I understand the question and I responsibly claim that in Zvornik we were a state within state. Whatever we did was done by the local people, and unfortunately these paramilitaries and volunteers, whatever you call them, they came for different reasons, for looting, hatred, and other reasons. So the leadership in Pale ... I mentioned Krajisnik here. On the 5th and the 6th, before all of it, he dropped by, and I asked him -- because we were confused with Arkan's men's arrival, he was very surprised, he didn't know about it, and he simply disappeared from Karakaj. I don't even know where he went. That's the answer more or less. No co-ordination could have existed and it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question by the Presiding Judge, can you read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Could there be or was there communication? Could one go to this Pale before Krajisnik arrived?"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the name?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Karisik, it's Karisik, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next page, please. And when you say "Krajisnik," you meant Karisik?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Karisik from the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How would you interpret it, an idiom in our language? Well, I really don't know, in the first few days everyone was minding their own business?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I answered already. Everyone was busy with themselves alone. All municipalities -- or perhaps let's not go into other municipalities, but in Zvornik, it was the local people who made decisions about everything of importance, for life, the conflict, the economy, everything, as if the state did not exist because it was only being established and even the basic state functions were not in place --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Can we see the previous page for the English. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karisik -- Mr. Ivanovic, when did Karisik arrive? When you referred to the period of chaos and ordering things after Karisik arrived, when were the Yellow Wasps arrested and when did Karisik impose order?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was in late July 1992. I don't know if I'm correct, but to the best of my recollection, late July or early August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have pages 17, 24, and 25 admitted, if that has not been tendered by Ms. McKenna already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll add those pages to the exhibit. Do we need to ask the CLSS to check the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would think we should and have the exhibit be corrected if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, what I was told is that what we have is the -- is an unrevised version of the OTP, so we hereby request the CLSS to take a look into this translation. Shall we continue. Yes, Ms. McKenna.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour, which -- because I believe the pages that Mr. Karadzic referred to are the B/C/S pages. Would that be pages 37 and 38 of the English? I just want to make sure that that whole discussion on communications is admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid I cannot be of assistance. I will rely on my associate, Mr. Sladojevic, he will inform the Prosecution of the page numbers in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to clarify, page 17 didn't relate to the discussion that we were just having.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we discussed is page 37 and 38 in e-court and hard copy as well, in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: In English, yes, Your Honour. But my understanding was that Mr. Karadzic asked for pages 17, 24, and 25 of the B/C/S. So I'm just making sure that we're all clear as to what exactly is being admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 38 in English was not something we touched upon. On page 17 we have something about what he was asked about in terms of how come it wasn't "no." And we clarified that Mr. Ivanovic stood by his answer that such things were done covertly without any PR. On 24 and 25, it has to do with the clarification of whether there was communication or not which is described by page -- on page 37 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But page 38 includes the conversation which Ms. McKenna discussed with the witness, so those pages will be -- we'll make sure that those pages are included in the exhibit. Shall we continue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that what's on page 38 was not shown to the witness, but very well, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. McKenna showed it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only the first two lines of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Ivanovic, you were asking about payments and the TO. Given the fact that you were the president of the peace time government in the joint municipality of Zvornik, can you tell us who was supposed to pay the municipal TO?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how people were being paid out by the municipality of Zvornik. I do know that -- that contributions were made by different companies in Zvornik, specifically in the company of Birac where I worked. There was money exempt for the procurement of food, clothes, footwear, and as well as some kind of payment or salary, although I believe they only received minimum amounts since we did not have enough money to pay out proper salaries to the armed forces. We were defending lives and freedom, and people were simply happy enough to have footwear, clothes, and a warm place to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for the paramilitary groups, did they arrive as paramilitaries and did they register themselves as volunteers with the TO?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I have been informed, I think they arrived as volunteers because there was no other way for them to arrive. They probably didn't like engaging in war and they didn't really come to be the true defenders of Serbian freedom, and then they cut themselves loose. They did what they wanted. No one could control them at the time. That's what I know about it, although I have no specific evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Zvornik government, was there someone who could deny payment to them?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think so. I think it all boiled down to force and threats. I don't know exactly how it worked. I don't want to tire you. I really don't know how much they pay these volunteers and if they pay them. I really know very little about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you said before, that there was no force, no person in power who could dare deny salaries to them, do you stand by that answer?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by it. They would get into factories with arms and rifles, and even if they walked into the municipal building with weapons, the last German mark, the last dinar would be paid out to them. It wasn't the payment of salaries; it was more taking the resources.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What we don't have in the transcript was that it wasn't the payment of salaries but it was simply seizing things, taking away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we have it here, taking the resources.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 95 of yesterday's transcript there was mention of a Muslim village where Serb forces entered. Can you say what you meant by that and whether it involved a lawful, legal formation; and if so, what unit was it?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall off-the-cuff what it had to do with. I can't say anything specifically in terms of what Serb forces they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it has to do with Djulici or another village that was abandoned by Muslim civilians. I was interested in what you meant to say when you said "Serb forces," was it on the basis of ethnicity or was it a legal formation commanded by the state?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no formation commanded by the state, they didn't exist at the time. The people involved were Serbs from the environs of Kladanj and Olovo. A large number of Serbs who with much effort and sacrifice managed to break through the encirclement of Muslim forces, since in Djulici, those people there felt it would be better for them to leave and stay alive than the others enter their homes. That's where they were accommodated. Those are the Serb forces. They included armed people from those areas, and thanks to the weapons they managed to break through and stay alive, otherwise they would all have been killed. That's where they found accommodation and the village population was supposed to go to Tuzla, and yesterday we discussed the issue of men being separated from the women and children. But I'd rather not go back to that issue again, but that's what I meant when I said "Serb forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 95 you mentioned that every village had its military leaders. Can you tell us under the Law on All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection, was it unlawful for every settlement, factory, let alone municipality to have their own TO --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Objection, objection, that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how -- who had the authority over the TO under the law?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A relative of mine was one of the leaders of people's defence and he explained to me how things worked. In Tito's Yugoslavia, which was falling apart at that time, it was the people who organised themselves in the case of natural disasters or whatever. This was a civil war, of course, it was not an external attack. But in such situations, any village organised its own defence. It was easy to understand it. No one had problems understanding it then. I don't know how clear I was now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you would be clearer if you spoke more slowly. Thank you. On page 97 yesterday, it was either read out to you or you said it. You mentioned some events, Brod, Sijekovac, Kupres, and so on, that affected the state of mind of the people in your area. Can you tell us what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Toward the end of 1991, much before or actually not much before, immediately before the events at Zvornik, because it was the end of the 20th century after all and there were communications in place and there hadn't yet been any extreme tensions, at that time atrocities were committed at Sijekovac. It's in the Brod municipality. The Croatian forces entered and committed crimes. At Kupres, too, I don't know what exactly the ethnic make-up of that area was. It was again the Croatian forces that committed terrible crimes, people were decapitated and what have you. And at another place, the Muslim forces committed crimes. And we weren't even aware that at Sapna a hundred men were armed and getting ready, whereas at the same time the Muslim authorities were telling us that everything was all right, that there were no problems, and so on. There was obviously distrust and somebody was giving orders to these people. Whether it was an order from the central authorities that came from Izetbegovic or not, I don't know. I suppose it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please repeat who the first victims were at the localities you mentioned because it wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All the victims were Serbs. At all these places I've mentioned, either Serbian civilians or JNA members. They were children, actually, not really soldiers. You couldn't really call them that, although they were wearing JNA soldiers -- JNA uniforms, which means they were the legal army of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 94 you were asked about the connections between the TO and the Crisis Staff. In the context of the arming implemented by the Crisis Staff. Did the JNA and the Crisis Staff arm individuals and what was the connection between the TO and the Crisis Staff? Did they distribute weapons to individuals and how was that regulated?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't know for sure how weapons were brought in, but I know that weapons did come in. I think that the Serbs got weapons -- well, where exactly did they come from? It may have been left behind by the JNA that was in Bosnia. The JNA went through to Serbia, but it seems that they left many weapons behind. I don't know how people obtained these weapons. They were distributed in villages, but I wasn't involved, so I'm not sure how it went. I never really asked. And the Muslims controlled the TO in Sarajevo and the police and then they were taking weapons from those storage facilities, but you know it was no problem getting weapons. Whenever people want weapons, they will get them, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did you activate the Serbian municipality of Zvornik so late? When was it proclaimed and when was it activated?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was proclaimed much earlier as a reaction to the impossibility of doing anything together. And when I say "together," I'm referring to the SDA party, that is, the Muslims of Zvornik. And it was activated, well, basically when the conflict began. We didn't want to activate it because it was ludicrous. We thought that we would be able to reach agreement. We believed that it would all end peacefully. We never even imagined there would be a conflict. It was a political response, a political platform, based on ignorance of what should be done. I believe that they too didn't know what to do, I'm talking about the executive authorities in Zvornik. But the first half here they probably didn't care much. They were preoccupied by the proclaiming of a sovereign Muslim Bosnia and probably by preparations, armed preparations. And I suppose that they wanted to get ready to exert control over us, but that's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In document P6404, on page 14 there is mention of this connection between the TO and the Crisis Staff in the context of the distribution of weapons. Now let us clarify what you meant --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it's page 15. It's page 15 in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Would you kindly repeat the page number, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, how much longer do you have? If it's more than five or ten minutes, the Chamber wishes to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Less than five minutes, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have to display the document. It was shown yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it because we have admitted only those limited number of pages? I'm told that it does not have 15 pages. Let us check. It's part of his October 2002 statement. Do we have a 65 ter number, then?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 25117.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That exists too, but it's another document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is 25117, the Exhibit number is P6402. What statement was -- is it? Is it March or October, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 15th of March and the 27th of March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivanovic, we read here that the variant involving the creation of two municipalities was successful. Was it possible for either ethnic community to be expelled from its municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCKENNA
utterances.text: Could I also request a specific reference from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's coming, but what passage is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's not from the document. On page 87 of yesterday's transcript, Mr. Ivanovic was asked about the municipality and he replied that everything was set for it to start working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And my question is: Would it have begun operating if everything had ended peacefully and would each side have gotten its own municipality?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would have continued to live peacefully with each other, which is the situation we have today, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is there a Muslim municipality of Zvornik today, whatever it's called?

utterances.speaker: JOVAN IVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No more questions, Mr. Ivanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Ivanovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. We'll rise all together. We'll have a break for half an hour and resume at five past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasilic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Vasilic, I must draw your attention to a certain rule of evidence that we have here at the International Tribunal, that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic or the Prosecution or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that may amount to admission of guilt in a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and, as a consequence, you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you in any case save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand what I have just told you, Mr. Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please point it out to me when I don't make a pause between your answer and my question because we want everything to be recorded and that's why we should both speak slowly. Did you give the Defence team a statement?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D9610 from e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see your statement on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I would kindly ask for it to be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you read and sign the statement?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show the last page to the witness so that he may identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions again today, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There's one associated exhibit being offered. It has not been on our 65 ter list because we hadn't finished the interview of this witness at the time we filed that list, so we would ask that it be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Gustafson?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. No, no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll admit the statement as well as the associated exhibit. Shall we assign the numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. 1D9610, the statement, will be Exhibit D3693, and 1D7329 will be Exhibit D3694.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read out a summary of Mr. Marinko Vasilic's statement in English. [In English] Marinko Vasilic started working for the BH MUP in 1975. He performed all duties from a police officer to commander. In the political campaigns before the first multi-party elections in Zvornik, there was an escalation of nationalism and chauvinism in the rallies of the SDA party. Shortly after the elections of the new authorities, there were new appointments in the Zvornik public security station. Osman Mustafic was appointed chief of the SJB and Dragan Spasojevic as commander of the Zvornik SJB. After the Zvornik authorities were formed in 1991, there was a split between the SDA and SDS. The SDA had a clear policy of action with the goal of separating BH from the SFRY at any cost, while SDS policy operated towards the preservation of the existing state and reaching a peaceful solution to the problems. SDA leaders from Sarajevo put big pressure on Zvornik Muslim leadership and -- to create a unitary BH, regardless of the will of the Serbs in BH. In 1991, Assistant Commander Mehmed Sahbegovic told Marinko Vasilic that it was time for the Muslims to create their state of Bosnia and the Serbs would be a minority in it. The SDA in Zvornik worsened ethnic relations by out-voting and ignoring the needs of the Serbs in Zvornik. This reflected on the deterioration in the relations in the Zvornik Public Security Station between Muslim police officers and the Serbian police officers. Muslims grouped themselves in some offices and Serbs in others. When Serbs went out into the field during operative work, they were not welcome in villages and local communes where the Muslims lived. Political disagreement in the local authorities of Zvornik impacted ordinary people. Ethnically motivated arguments and incidents were all encouraged by Islamic extremists in the local authorities causing frequent physical attacks and maltreatment of Serbs and members of the JNA in the town by organised groups of Muslims. There were attacks on soldiers and officers, causing great fear among the Serbs. In early 1991, Muslim commanding officers in Zvornik SJB started forming reserve police stations. The stations were exclusively formed in the villages inhabited by only Muslims. They were issued with long-barrelled weapons. The weapons came through illegal channels from Sarajevo and Tuzla. The Serbs did not know of these activities and insisted on talks and issued various statements calling on good neighbourly relations with mutual respect. They wanted to resolve problems peacefully. The Serbs saw the JNA as a force and institution which could prevent a civil war in BH. In summer 1991, the SDS organised a rally in support of peace in Zvornik. Radovan Karadzic and other SDS leaders spoke at the rally. All speakers asked everyone to make an effort and showing a maximum tolerance and condemning nationalism and separatism reach a peaceful solution through talks. The Muslims took the police station in Zvornik twice. Leaders of the Zvornik SDA were responsible for taking the station and setting up barricades in the town and in Muslim villages. As the security situation deteriorated every day, the JNA carried out mobilisation preventing a potential ethnic conflict in Zvornik. The Serbs responded to mobilisation while the Muslims, under pressure from their leaders, boycotted this mobilisation and portrayed the JNA as the occupying army. At the time, the Muslims already had armed units. By 3rd of April, 1992, Muslim paramilitary units set up many check-points and barricades throughout Zvornik. On 5th of April, Muslim extremists killed a JNA officer, causing panic and fear among the Serbs. In populated areas or villages where Serbs lived, people formed village guards on their own initiative to protect themselves. On 6th of April, 1992, Zvornik was sealed off and under full control of Muslims. Serbs who did not pull out during the night started fleeing to Karakaj individually. Armed Muslims were controlling the town. They searched Serbian houses and apartments, maltreating and beating the Serbs who were there. The Serbian leadership in Zvornik continued talks that had already been started and initiated a meeting with the Muslim leadership for security reasons. Jovo Mijatovic and Jovo Ivanovic joined the team for talks on behalf of the Serbs. Arkan burst uninvited into the meeting in Mali Zvornik with his men. He called the Serbian negotiators traitors, saying they had no right to sell Serbian land. A soldier beat both Serbian negotiators. Arkan and his unit then took over command and influenced everything that happened in Zvornik. In late April 1992, Marinko Vasilic tried to organise police work with the goal to -- of ensuring security for the people of Zvornik. They set up check-points and tried to secure the vital buildings in the town. There was no electricity or telephone lines, so communication was organised through couriers. The local Serbian authorities in Zvornik were powerless to oppose the anarchy and lawlessness of the paramilitary units in Zvornik. Police officers were often physically maltreated and abused by the paramilitaries. They tried to get out of their way whenever possible. Both local and police leadership were left to the mercy of the paramilitary forces. The local leadership tried and took some actions to alleviate the extreme and arrogant activity of the paramilitaries as much as it could. Marinko Vasilic repeatedly asked his colleagues in Mali Zvornik for help with paramilitary groups and individuals. None of his requests came to fruition. In July 1992 Branko Grujic informed Radovan Karadzic about Zvornik's problems. Karadzic was surprised by the situation in Zvornik. He ordered police forces be sent to Zvornik and arrest the gang. Shortly after, Branko Grujic and Marinko Vasilic submitted irrevocable resignation for fear of their lives and lives of their families. On 29th and 30th of July of 1992, special forces of the MUP came to Zvornik, in co-ordinated military action with military police units and, using weapons, arrested paramilitary units. All the persons arrested were prosecuted and tried before the relevant courts in RS and Serbia. And that is short summary, and at that moment I do not have questions for Mr. Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I was waiting for the French translation to be completed. Yes, Mr. Vasilic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its entirety in writing, that is, through your written witness statement. And now you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that? Yes, Ms. Gustafson. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasilic.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 2 of your statement you refer to statements you've given to the Office of the Prosecution in the past, but I think your dates are a little off. One of the statements you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor was a tape-recorded statement that you gave in October of 2002 in Zvornik. That's right, isn't it? You spoke to the OTP on tape in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I talked to the representatives of this Tribunal, investigators, but I don't remember the year. I think it was soon after this Tribunal was established, that it's actually the 1990s, I think. It was in Zvornik at that, at the courthouse. After a while in Zvornik at the Vidikovac motel. I think my headphones are going to fall off.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that -- the interview that you gave to the OTP, the second one, was tape recorded and the transcript clearly indicates that the date was October of 2002. Do you agree at least that in 2002, 11 years ago, your memory of events in 1992 was better than it is today?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to challenge the year because it's been a lot of time since then, and I know that I talked to the investigators. But the content of that conversation was that then. Perhaps somebody could remind me what the content was then and what it is now. Maybe I could give an explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, could you come closer to the microphone so that the interpreters could hear you better? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, don't worry about the contents of that interview now. Rest assured, we will be going through some of the contents of that interview in the examination. Right now I just wanted to get some basic facts about it. And do you agree that your memory of events in 1992 -- sorry, your memory of events from 1992 was better 11 years ago than it is today?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that some details were fresher in my mind then, but I don't know what this is about. It is certain that my memory was fresher then than it is now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement you explain that in late April 1992, after Dragan Spasojevic left the police, you became commander of the Zvornik Public Security Station. Before that and before the war broke out in Zvornik, you were an assistant commander in the Zvornik SJB; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And then, as you said in your statement, you became commander in April 1992. And then in early June 1992 you became the Zvornik SJB chief, replacing Milos Pantelic; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's right too, but I don't know whether the date is accurate. It doesn't really matter. But in principle, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you resigned from the position of chief of the SJB and left the police in late July 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
