utterances.text: You speak at length in your statement about the arming and other preparations for war carried out by the Muslim side in Zvornik, and you contrast that with the Serb side. You said that the Serbs "fully believed that there would be no war and insisted on talks and agreement with a view to resolving the problems peacefully." So is it your position that the Serbs in Zvornik were not arming or preparing for war? Or do you accept that, in fact, both sides were arming and preparing for war in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Whether both sides were arming and preparing for war? That's a very delicate question. It is one thing to prepare for war and to wage it, and it's another thing to arm yourself and defend yourself. The Serbs -- well, I'm not saying that they were not arming themselves, but the very fact that Serbs trusted the JNA, believing that they would be the guarantor of safety and security and of averting a war, that makes it more likely for them not to be arming themselves to such a high degree at all. On the other hand, you have this striking statement, astonishing statement, by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, who says that he is -- that he is prepared to sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina. That fact in itself says who is in favour of which variant. The Serbs were in favour of the survival of Yugoslavia, including Bosnia-Herzegovina, both the Serbs and Muslims, whereas the leaders of the SDA were --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: -- in favour of the secession of this republic. That would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to ask you to try to focus your answers as much as possible on the specific question I ask because my time is limited. Now, in your answer you're saying: "I'm not saying that they weren't arming themselves," referring to the Serb side. In 2002, you told the Office of the Prosecutor that both the Serb side and the Muslim side were arming and preparing for war, and I refer to 65 ter 25215, pages 46, 47, and 71. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying it now either. Serbs -- certain Serbs got ahold of weapons in a certain way and that's what I said before too, but I'm talking about the people as a whole, the people as a whole. There are extreme individuals, extremists, in the -- within the Serb people too, and they showed their true face during the course of this war too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit P2591 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Vasilic, you are aware that in the months before the conflict broke out the Serbian municipality of Zvornik passed a decision forming a Serbian municipality which listed territories that formed part of that Serbian municipality? You're aware of that decision, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that decision. I heard that there was talk about the division of Zvornik between the Serbs and Muslims, where Serbs were a majority, that should belong to the Serbs, and where Muslims were a majority, that should belong to them. But as for an official decision, I do not remember having stated anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me remind you of what you said in 2002 when you were shown this document that's on the screen before you now. You were asked: "Do you recall this decision?" And this is at page 44. And you said: "Just a second. I heard of it but I didn't see it before." That's what you told the OTP in 2002 and that's accurate; right? You'd heard of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Well, it's possible that I heard of it. I'm not going to say it never existed, but I'm just telling you that the intention was -- I mean that I heard that political representatives were discussing a peaceful settlement, ultimately a division of the municipality of Zvornik. I'm not denying I said that either, but allow for the possibility that I've forgotten. I don't know who compiled this decision. I did not take part in this, so it is possible that I heard of it and that I forgot about it in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to look at the territories listed under item 2, which is in the middle of the page in the B/C/S, and it's at the bottom of page 1 and the top of page 2 in the English. And I'm going to remind you of what you said in 2002 about this. You were asked: "In part 2 of this, the areas that were comprised Serbian municipality of Zvornik, that is around 63 areas, can you tell me what proportion of the municipality that would have made up? Do you understand? Can you tell me, looking at these areas that are listed, what percentage or proportion of the municipality would be covered by those areas listed?" And you say: "In a territorial sense?" And the investigator says: "Yes." And you say: "I would say 80 per cent." Now, that's what you told the OTP in 2002 with respect to the territories listed under item 2 of the document on the screen in front of you, that those areas comprise roughly 80 per cent of the territory of Zvornik. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't want to deal with percentages because I'm not an expert in that field, but I know for sure that in the territory of the municipality of Zvornik, land, as such, was owned by Serbs for the most part. In relation to land ownership by Muslims. Although the ratio of Serb and Muslim population is 60 to 40 per cent in favour of the Muslims. So now if we were to look at the map of the municipality of Zvornik from Bijeljina towards this side, if we're going to look at the area, you know you can paint the map and then you'd see that most of this territory would belong to the Serbs if that kind of agreement were reached on that kind of division, 70, 60, whatever. Don't take my word for it. I'm not a land surveyor or something. I mean, it's one thing to talk under these circumstances and it was a different situation to talk in that situation. You know, I guess you understand what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Not exactly. Are you saying you didn't tell the truth in 2002 when you talked to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: No, I did not say that I was not telling the truth, but I did not know whether it was 80 or 60 per cent. Maybe that just came out, you know, uncontrolled. To this day I don't know what the ratio would be, if there were to be this kind of division, what would belong to the Serb side and what would belong to the Muslim side. Then it would have to be dealt with by experts from that field. So the then-politicians or leaders would agree in order to find a compromise.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you then about some of the specific territories listed in item 2 here. Sopotnik, which was listed in item 2, that was a majority Muslim village. According to the 1991 census there were 189 Muslims and 68 Serbs; right? That was a Muslim village predominantly?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Sopotnik, there are two Sopotniks, a Muslim Sopotnik and a Serb Sopotnik. And when these people asked me about that, I assume that I said probably the Serb part of Sopotnik would belong to the Serbs. Not at any moment did it cross my mind that the Muslim part should belong to Serb Sopotnik. And finally, after all, allow me to say that I'm not a politician. I did not take part in the creation of these talks. I did not take part in these talks. I was a policeman --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: -- who possibly answered these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You've been asked again to move closer to the microphone so the interpreters can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right now I'm just asking you about the ethnic make-up of some of these villages. Donji Grbavci, that was also a majority Muslim village? 846 Muslims and 206 Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which Donji Grbavci? What is meant by Donji Grbavci? There are villages and there are hamlets, Hajdarevici, Lupici, but also there are Serb villages that are linked there, Kitovnice, part of Jardan. I have already given you an answer. Please don't. I know what the ratio is of the population in the municipality of Zvornik. It was about 60 per cent in favour of the Muslims and 40 per cent in favour of the Serbs. Perhaps there was 1 or 2 percentage points accounting for some other ethnic communities. But for you to ask me about the percentage of the population in different villages, I mean I really cannot answer those questions for you. Although I might have said something over there, but I'm not the one who was doing that arithmetic and came up with a solution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I tender the pages that contain the passages I read out to the witness regarding his comments on this document. It's pages 43 and 44 of 65 ter 251 -- 25215, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6405, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you're -- if you are tendering this exhibit in the future, I'd like to see the passage as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasilic, you are also aware, although you don't mention this in your statement, that the Zvornik Crisis Staff declared a state of war in Zvornik on the 6th of April, 1992. That's something else you said in 2002 to the OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Possibly, I don't remember. But as far as I can remember, Republika Srpska -- rather, at the time what was the name of Republika Srpska? The Republic of the Serb people, was it, in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Possibly I said that for Zvornik in view of the Crisis Staff, that it existed. So I found that logical. If there is a Crisis Staff and if there is shooting, then nothing different can be said except that there was a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 25215, specifically page 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: AND, Mr. Vasilic, you were shown the document in which the Crisis Staff declared a state of war in Zvornik, which is P3154 in this case. And you were asked: "Do you recall the declaration of the state of war in Zvornik?" And you said: "I didn't see it. I heard of it because you know of my position at the time." What you told the OTP in 2002 was that you hadn't seen the decision but you'd heard of it because of your position in the police at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In lines 9 onwards where the witness spoke about the state of war, it was not recorded that Republika Srpska did not declare a state of war. [In English] Before the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: -- "possibly I said for Zvornik ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, not denying something is different than accepting it. Do you accept that you heard about the declaration of the state of war in Zvornik at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: If I stated that then, I'm telling you now after all these years -- well, probably, probably that is the case. I'm not denying that. I mean, I cannot remember each and every word that I uttered. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page as well in light of the witness's somewhat ambivalent answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasilic, you said in your statement in paragraph 21 that in the period leading up to the outbreak of war in Zvornik, the Serbs formed village guards on their own initiative, but you also knew that on the 8th of April, 1992, the Crisis Staff ordered a general mobilisation in Zvornik. You were aware of that order too, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 63 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Vasilic, you were shown the general mobilisation order, which is P3381 in this case, and you said -- you were informed: "This is an order on general mobilisation." And you were asked: "Mr. Vasilic, do you recall this order?" And you said: "The same as the previous one, heard of it, and I didn't see it." Do you accept now that you heard about the general mobilisation order at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: If I said so back then, I accept it, although I don't recall that. I accept it. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. You refer to Arkan's activities and his presence in Zvornik at the outbreak of the conflict. And one thing that you don't say in your statement that you've said before was that when Arkan's men were in Zvornik, for the first four or five days they were based in the Alhos building in Karakaj, in the same building where the police and Crisis Staff were also based. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes. But would you kindly allow me to clarify something? President Karadzic read my statement. He read out the summary. I would kindly ask for specific details so that I can explain. As for Arkan's unit being at Alhos with us, it doesn't mean, it cannot mean, that we thought they were precious and could hardly await their arrival. But might makes right and they did not bother to ask for our opinion. It is a fact that they were in the nearby offices and we were across the hall.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said that they represented the force that did not ask for our opinion --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Might makes right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please kindly slow down and approach the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, you're again being asked to speak -- to move closer to the microphone. Now, at paragraph 29 of your statement you said that on the 9th of April, 1992, Arkan and his forces relieved the blockade of Zvornik, and you referred to Arkan and his unit taking over command. When you testified in the Grujic case, however, you said that the town of Zvornik was liberated by the Zvornik TO "with the help of Arkan's men." That's 65 ter 25217 at page 108. That's right, isn't it, Mr. Vasilic? This was a joint operation involving not just Arkan's men but the Zvornik TO as well?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I'll respond to the question but do allow me to finish. Arkan with his unit -- well, Pejo, his man, asked of us to have some of our men at their disposal since a day or two previously we could not ensure that, he cursed us and left. And then that day or that date, on the 2nd, Arkan came with his men and then he carried out this additional manning of the unit he planned to establish comprising the people of Karakaj and Celopek. And so he did the job in Zvornik with them. They were Serbs, locals who were in some kind of -- well, they were the people who stood guard on the Serb side. Later on, when the TO was organised and when the VRS was organised, certainly those people were made part of the VRS, and I have in mind the inhabitants of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, it was a very simple question. I'm going to ask it again because you didn't answer it. In the Grujic case you said that the town of Zvornik was liberated by the Territorial Defence of the town of Zvornik with the help of Arkan's men. Were you telling the truth when you gave that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I always tell the truth. If only I were always allowed to explain. I told the gentlemen in Belgrade, especially attorney Todorovic when he tried to explain that there had been an aggression carried out, but it's not possible for a hundred or 200 volunteers from Serbia could present such a force that would be able to carry out an act of aggression, whereas the Serbs in Zvornik municipality had several thousand of our men who were later on placed in military formations. Well, that is why I'm trying to explain it to you now. It is a fact that they were members of the TO, but it was not organised then. But I simply use the expression "members of the TO."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 25217, page 108 of the English and page 73 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Vasilic, this is right at the bottom of the page in both languages. You're being asked about the operation in the town of Zvornik and you were asked: "What was it liberated from and who liberated it?" And you answer: "It was liberated by the Territorial Defence of the town of Zvornik." And the Judge says: "Face the Panel." And then you add: "With the help, with the help of Arkan's men." I'm going to ask you one more time. That's what you said in the Grujic case and that's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: It is true that Arkan, with his men, led the operation and that the people from Karakaj assisted him. That would be the real truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6406, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, this isn't discussed anywhere in your statement, but you are aware, are you not, that during the time when you were police station commander and police station chief, there were some terrible, terrible crimes committed against Muslims in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go through some of the things you've said about these crimes in your prior statements and ask you to confirm them. So in 2002 -- first I'm going to ask you about the massacre in Drinjaca at the end of May 1992. And you told the OTP in 2002 that you received information from the reserve police officers in Drinjaca that a TO unit under the command of Lieutenant Martic executed a group of Muslim prisoners in the school playground in Drinjaca. And that's pages 114, 115, and 119. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: It is true that the event took place. It is true that a certain Lieutenant, not Martic but Matic, that person had a group of men who came from outside Bosnia and Herzegovina. They went to the area of Drinjaca where they carried out independent operations. In their operations, of course, some inhabitants of Drinjaca participated, but I don't know who they were. It all went through this kid, Lieutenant Matic. Later on I inquired who he was and where he had come from. I was told he was a lieutenant and that he was somewhere in the area of Vitinice -- or, actually, that he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter -- sorry -- yeah, 65 ter 25215, page 114.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You were asked about the killing in Drinjaca and you said -- you were asked: "What can you tell us?" And you say, this is at the bottom of the page: "I don't remember precisely who informed me. Was it Ljubisav, Ljubisa, or someone else, but we did receive information that the men were taken to the stadium and they were lined, so to speak, lined up just like in the army, and then in the end Territorial Defence member Lieutenant Martic and his group of people shot them. I'm not sure if that's the appropriate expression, but the women were present when that happened. They were watching." And then at page 119 you were asked: "You said that Martic and his men were responsible, so how do you ..." and then there's something incomprehensible. And then you say: "I learned -- I heard that from the police officers who worked there and that was also the rumour in the town." Now, Mr. Vasilic, Lieutenant Martic, it may have been a mistake and it's actually Lieutenant Matic, but you say clearly that he was a Territorial Defence unit commander. And that's true, right, that was the information you had?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, he was the commander of his unit, of his group of men. They were joined by some people from the area. I think that the TO commander was a different person. I don't know his name, but the person in question was from the area. I could even speculate that he was a certain Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have a Serbian version of this so that the witness could see his own words in the Serbian language and what they were?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We only have English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, you also told the OTP that Lieutenant Matic -- that you'd heard that he was an active officer of the JNA and that he came to the area after withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's possible. I think after so much time I really -- I know that he was not from Zvornik municipality and I never saw him. I heard his name was Lieutenant Matic and that he was not even from BiH.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I can't even deny that he was a military person. I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, let me remind --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript. The witness did not say "I can't deny." He said "I cannot assert that he was not a military person of the VJ."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So let me remind you of what you said in 2002, and that's on the previous page, page 118, near the bottom you were asked about Lieutenant Martic or Matic, as we now know, and his unit. And you said: "I don't know for sure but I heard that he was an active officer of JNA and that he came to this area after withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia." And then you were asked: "At the time, where did his unit fit in? What was it ..." And you said on the next page: "I think that at that time brigade was still not formed. I believe that time that Territorial Defence units were organising different settlements or locations, their companies, platoons, and so on, but they were all subordinated to the Territorial Defence commander." So --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and I say so now as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And you also told the OTP that: "At the time there was a reserve police station located in the Drinjaca Dom Kulture commanded by Ljubisav Petrovic." That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And also in 2002, the investigators told you that their information about this massacre was that the males who were executed were held in the Drinjaca Dom Kulture with the women and children and then the men were taken out and executed on the nearby playground. And you responded that: "If that was the case, the police who were stationed in the Dom Kulture in Drinjaca must have known all the details of this massacre." And that's right, isn't it, if the massacre took place right outside the Dom Kulture, the police officers stationed in Dom Kulture would have known all about it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: If you allow me, I was asked, first of all, and they asserted that it actually happened in the cultural hall and that the reserve police station was located in the building, which is incorrect. The reserve police or milicija station, as it was called then, as far as I know was placed in the cultural hall in Drinjaca. The cultural hall is physically separate from the school. And if the policemen were there, if not -- if they were not able to see it, they could have heard it. But you will allow that I said earlier in an investigation and that it was conveyed by Ljubisav or Ljubisa Petrovic that it took place under such circumstances so not in the cultural hall and not immediately next to the cultural hall. Now, whether they saw it, whether they observe it from somewhere, I really can't say. When it comes to the reserve police station, since we are on that topic, any bigger local commune or several local communes across Zvornik municipality had reserve police stations --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: -- and joint reserve police stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the structure of reserve police stations in Zvornik. I'd like to ask you to please focus on the specific questions I ask.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 120 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And here you were asked -- you were told by the investigator: "The information we have is that the execution was -- those people were held in 'Dom Kulture,' and that it would have included men and women, and that men were taken outside and executed on a basketball court outside 'Dom Kulture' in groups of about 10. Can you tell us something about that?" And you say: "I don't know about those details." And you were asked: "If that was the case, it was just outside 'Dom Kulture,' it would have been just outside your reserve police office; is that correct?" And you said: "It was surely not far." And the question was asked: "It was on a basketball court. You know the basketball court I'm talking about?" And you answer: "I don't think there are two. There is a playground or field or football field in front of the school. I think that's the only one. Is it a basketball court or something else, I don't know." And then the investigator says: "So the information we have is that they were executed there. If that was the case, your police would have to be well aware of what took place." And you answered: "Most probably they were there and they were watching the whole thing from the building. They must know the details." That's what you said in 2002 and that's the truth; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: If I said so, although I cannot recall the details, whether it was precisely conveyed word for word, then I do not dispute it if the policemen were there. If they were there, if they could not see every detail, then at least they could have heard what was going on. I do not deny that. But I can't say that it was so word for word. I don't know what the distance is, and I reply that any school had some kind of pitch and it would be one rather than two. Now, whether the policemen were there, how many were there, how many were in the field, I don't know. If they were there, they could have observed -- seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- your answer is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at page 115 of this transcript, you were asked about what happened after this, and I'd like to read the question and answer to you. You were asked: "So what happened to these people being killed? Did you make any inquiry afterwards?" And you said: "Nothing was done there." And another question started to be asked and then you continued, you said: "Except ... nothing but again, typical conversations with leading men in the staff and leading politicians. It was said that things could no longer go that way, could be run that way, and that that was no longer war. But it was much more horrific than a regular war. There was no response. There were no questions asked. All normal people were very surprised and very depressed by this." And that's the truth, isn't it, Mr. Vasilic? You raised this massacre with leading politicians and leading men in the staff. There was no response and nothing was done; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I broached this topic with the gentleman in the TO staff so that we would see what happened, why it happened, and how it developed, and who was responsible. However, the Chief of Staff promised to investigate it. As for other facilities where people were being taken to, I insisted that people could not be taken to unless it is known who was being brought in, by whom, and why --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about other facilities now. I'm asking you about this massacre in Drinjaca. And in 2002 you said you spoke to leading politicians and leading men in the staff and there was no response and nothing was done. Was that the truth that you said in 2002 or were you lying?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Madam, I never lied. Please don't use that term. I'm telling you, and I repeat, that I discussed the topic with the TO staff chief, Mr. Marko Pavlovic. It was Marko Pavlovic at the time and I didn't know what other names he went by. I didn't know who he was or where he had come from. He promised to investigate the case. Under the Law on the Armed Forces of the former Yugoslavia, all acts committed by members of the army or Territorial Defence are to be investigated by the competent organs of the unit or district. That is why I no longer dealt with the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, you say you never lied, but you just said twice now that Marko Pavlovic promised to investigate this incident, and in 2002 you said there was no response and nothing was done. One of those statements is a lie, which one?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I ask you again, it's not a lie, do not use that term. I told you he promised me. Now, as for him not doing anything, you should ask him about it. I was in no position to force Mr. Marko Pavlovic or arrest him for not having done it. If you will allow me, I can tell you about my past and my relationship with such forces that were killing in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about that --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Because no one would listen to me on that score.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is it your position now that Marko Pavlovic promised to investigate this incident, but in fact did nothing? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm trying to tell you and to explain to you. The man promised it would be investigated to see what happened, how it happened, and why. It was up to the security organs to investigate the case. Whether anything was done, I don't know. I have no feedback. That's why I said the result is zero, nothing was done.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 12, the witness said that it was up to the security organ and he had a security organ, that is the TO or Mr. Pavlovic, that is his security organ, which was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know what part is the -- what witness actually said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 12 of page 68 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, because I think you seem to have added your explanation. So, Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. We can have the recording reviewed. It was up to the security organ, and what's missing is that he had a security organ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. If you stopped there it was clear, but you added some explanation as if those explanation were also his words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, but I wanted to explain the meaning which was lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender this page of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this page as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, you also told the OTP in 2002 what you knew about the execution of men from the Djulici area, in the Karakaj technical school, and Gero's slaughter-house. And you said that you heard about the killings of these men immediately after these events because this was the talk of the town at the time. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: After the events themselves, I did not hear that and I can't have stated anything of the kind. I know how those persons came to the technical school, if we're talking about the people from Djulici, or rather, Bijeli Potok.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you about right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 96 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the bottom you were asked: "Now, this information that you've received about the killing of people at Karakaj technical school or Gero's, who did you receive that from?" And you said: "It was the rumour of the town." And on the next page you were asked: "But whom did you receive it from?" You said: "I don't remember! It was too long ago." And you were asked: "When, when did you hear of that?" And you said: "That was talked about for about half a year, and I guess I heard about it immediately after the events had taken place, and the more free the town became, the more people talked about this." Now, that's true, isn't it, Mr. Vasilic, this was the talk of the town immediately after the events and you heard about it immediately after the events; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's a mistake. It's a mistake made in the explanation. I said that I had heard of these misdeeds after leaving the police, that is, a few months later. In other words, I didn't hear it immediately, after a day or two or five, but a few months later. That's when I heard of Celopek, the technical school centre, after the arrest of the paramilitaries who were taken to prison. That's how it was. For a couple of months, it was the whisper of the town rather than the talk because no one dared speak out loud about it. Even after those persons had been arrested, no one dared speak openly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, the Chamber just heard this morning from another Defence witness who confirmed that this is what everybody was talking about immediately after the events, the killing of hundreds of men from the Karakaj technical school, and he said that he heard about it within days. You were either the police station commander or the police chief at the time these killings took place. Are you saying that you didn't know what everyone was talking about in Zvornik at the time, about this horrible crime?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That is correct --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we get a reference for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is a reference to what the previous witness said and how he said it?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't have it at my finger-tips. It was my recollection from sitting in court this morning, but I will find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, I'm not sure we got your entire answer. Are you -- do you agree that you as police station commander or police station chief did not know about this massacre even though this was what everyone was talking about in Zvornik at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. The events or the massacre at the secondary school centre at Karakaj or the Celopek case, I faced Mr. Sredo Vukovic in Belgrade at the special court and I faced Mr. Petko Panic and they changed their statement given to that same court because they stated that they had thought that I knew, or that Sredo Vukovic said that I had told that certain people were to be transferred to Celopek from Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: -- in no case --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. This is not responsive to my question. You're being asked about what you knew and when you knew it. I'm not asking you about what other people said in other trials. It's about what you knew and when you knew it.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you now so you can find the documents and see that I'm not lying, that I'm telling the truth. I did not know about these events. I found out several months later, and even then people whispered about it. The people who knew immediately either were involved or something else. There were about -- you almost -- ten groups of paramilitaries. You didn't dare breathe let alone comment. I don't know who had that much courage; I didn't. If I had known of such things, you can trust me that I wouldn't have remained silent. When I exhausted all possibilities of removing the paramilitaries, I asked President Grujic that --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: -- that we should go to meet President Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: -- and apply for help. That's your reply: I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you once again to just answer the question I ask you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I would like to tender pages 100 -- 96 and 97 and have that added to the existing exhibit number. And I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that. Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The witness said: "And we went to meet President Karadzic and ask for assistance," not "we should go," line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just -- Dr. Karadzic has asked for the transcript reference for the question I put. It was page 7, lines 12 to 22 of this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, do you have anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just understood the precise line reference was 17 to 23. That was the only thing I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll break for 45 minutes and resume at 20 past 1.00 -- I'm sorry, 20 past 12.00 -- oh, 20 past 1.00. I'm carried away. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, before the break I was asking you about your knowledge of the massacre of men from Djulici at the Karakaj technical school and Gero's slaughter-house. I have one more question about this event, these events, which was -- which is to have you confirm what you said to the OTP in 2002, which was that nothing was done to investigate these killings. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 46 of your statement you refer to events in Celopek. Somewhat elliptically you state that the reserve police members who provided security there never informed you about events that took place there. You're talking here about the Celopek Dom Kulture, where reserve police officers guarded some Muslim civilians who were kept there; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you testified in the Grujic case that those Muslims were taken to the Celopek Dom Kulture on Drinatrans buses on the orders of either the TO staff or the interim government and they were escorted there by police official Miko Miljanovic. That's what you said and that's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you about the paramilitary groups in Zvornik. You described them as being too powerful for the police to oppose. And I want to ask you about one of those units which was known as Gogic's men. Now, you told the OTP in 2002 that they were brought in when Milos Pantelic was the police chief, they wore police uniforms, and they were paid by the municipality within the police organisation. That's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: It's accurate, but I would like to explain that if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could briefly -- if there's something you feel you need to explain to make sense of your answer, please do so briefly.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. Just that this Trial Chamber knows where those people came from. When Milos Pantelic became the station chief, he brought these people with him. And I asked him, "Who are these people? Where are they from?" And he answered, "These are my men, they are under my control." And then I said, "There can't be two police forces in one police station." When they came they were wearing camouflage uniforms and on their shoulders there was a police patch. I insisted that these people be removed, and he answered that I had nothing to do with them, that they were under his authority, and that he was in charge. I was trying to get rid of these paramilitaries and I included the Gogic's men in that group. I asked the people from Mali Zvornik and Serbia for assistance because they were -- most of them were from Serbia or almost all of them. And once we nearly succeeded or --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once we succeeded but they returned. As for the fact that they were paid by the municipality, we were all because it didn't function otherwise. And Chief Pantelic insisted that a list be made of all police personnel and that these people be put on the list, and that's how they got paid.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your answer you referred several times to Milos Pantelic telling you that Gogic's men were his men, they were under his control, under his authority, and that, the fact that Gogic's men were operating under the direct authority and control of the police chief at the time, was one of the reasons that it was difficult for the police to oppose this unit. How could they oppose this unit if they were operating under the direct authority of the police chief? That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You talk in your statement about how difficult it was for the police to oppose these paramilitary units. With respect to Gogic's men, one of the reasons it was difficult to oppose them is because they were operating under the authority and control of the police chief; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I opposed them. The others didn't because they expected me to do, and naturally I did but Chief Pantelic insisted that they were under his authority and that they reported exclusively to him. And I said that there couldn't be two police forces. Some people were to report both to me and him and others only to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And one of the things that concerned you about this group and caused you to complain to Chief Pantelic was that Gogic's men were behaving in an obviously improper way. That's what you told the OTP in 2002 and that's true; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you had fears about how Gogic's men would treat civilians, given your observations of them. That's another thing you told the OTP and that's true; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: It's true that people were -- the people were getting drunk, that they were behaving arrogantly. Simply, there was no -- they were out of control. They were present but they were not controlled. And the same could be expected from them as from the other paramilitaries who were present, and I can tell this Trial Chamber that at the moment while groups were coming in, the people thought that they were coming to help, but then the population soon realised that they hadn't arrived for the interest of the Serbian people but for their own interest and frivolously.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement at paragraph 36 you said that you were left to the mercy of these paramilitaries thanks to the poor or non-existent communication with the relevant republican organs. So my question for you is this: When was the first time that you communicated to the republican MUP authorities the problems you were having with paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise date. First and foremost, we didn't have means of communication such as phone lines, telexes, and what have you. It took quite some time to set up radio communications and other channels of communication. People from the ministry did call at us, but it seems to me that the real reason was for them to take their families to Serbia where they were safe and that they just dropped by in passing. I explained to them that it was impossible to work here, even live here. And there were some promises made that they would forward this information up the ladder so that these paramilitaries be eliminated. And I went to Mali Zvornik to ask for help with Brano Grujic, as I've already said, but unsuccessfully --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to stop you because we're moving away from the question. Let me remind you what you said in your Grujic case testimony. You told the Trial Chamber that: "MUP inspectors from the Sarajevo MUP came to Zvornik several times in May and June 1992" and that you told them about the problems that you were having. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said now too, that people from the ministry came, but it was my impression that they called only in passing, to see what was happening, and I explained my problem to them. Later on when communications became operational again, when it was possible to send out documents, and I remember a report of mine where I described the problem with paramilitaries in the Zvornik area, we were almost kept prisoner in the headquarters, we were hiding from the paramilitaries headed by Zuco. We were detained for five hours at gunpoint. Well, that's quite enough for you to understand who you're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's in your statement, and again you're moving away from the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have D1436, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Vasilic, do you recall an inspection carried out at the Zvornik SJB by Dragomir Andan and Danilo Vukovic between -- sometime between the 29th of May and the 12th of June, 1992? Mr. Vasilic, did you hear the question? This document states that an inspection was carried out by Dragomir Andan and Danilo Vukovic from the two MUP inspectors of the Zvornik SJB between 29 May and 12 June 1992. Do you recall this inspection?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: There was a number of -- there were a number of people. There was Mr. Andan and others, but I don't recall their names. On two or three occasions people came, but I don't remember the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, this is the part of the report discussing the inspection in Zvornik and I'd like to direct you to the second paragraph in the B/C/S, if it could be made as large as possible. And this is the first page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the report states: "Even on the territory of liberated area of Zvornik, the SJB Zvornik comes across numerous problems regarding the visit and activities by paramilitary formation in this area. Besides the fact that the government of Zvornik municipality has through its decision banned the establishment of a training camp run by Captain Dragan, military authorities have allowed that the same be formed in the area of Divici. According to the senior staff at the SJB Zvornik, the same have also usurped the premises of Vidikovac hotel and have gathered there a large number of persons criminally inclined, persons prone to robbery, terror, rapes, et cetera. Due to such a decision and legalisation of the stay by criminally inclined persons in this area, the chief of SJB Zvornik, dissatisfied with the decision by military authorities, has submitted a request to be released from his duty." And in the next paragraph it states: "It is necessary to mention that these persons have on multiple occasions confiscated tools, foreign currency and other valuables, committed rapes, and even killed Muslim nationals who were ready for exchange." Mr. Vasilic, in your statement you attributed the problems with paramilitaries to poor or non-existent communication with republican organs. But this report by a republican organ indicates that this is not a communication problem. The republican authorities are clearly aware of the situation in Zvornik. The problem, as stated in this report, is that the military authorities in Zvornik are protecting and supporting the paramilitaries. That's the gist of the complaints of the Zvornik SJB as recorded here; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the military authorities were supporting the paramilitaries. I can neither confirm nor deny that. But they didn't get approval from the military authorities to set up a training centre at Vidikovac, but Captain Dragan did that on his own. He came to talk to me and Mr. Grujic. And we told Captain Dragan, Frankly, if you came to fight for the Serbian people, go to headquarters [as interpreted] and see the commander rather than request computers and I don't know what kind of machines from us, that was out of the question. And then he wanted to establish a training centre. What has that got to do with us? It's not for us to either support it or not support it. The republican authorities were the ones who had the authority to give approval to that. I don't know who could have supported him. General Mladic once expelled him, he ordered him to leave Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript. [Interpretation] I apologise, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it's about the transcript. In line 12, it was wrongly recorded that Mr. Vasilic told Captain Dragan to go to headquarters, whereas the witness said "go to the brigade" rather than "headquarters."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, you just stated that Captain Dragan did not have authority from the military to set up his training camp. This contemporaneous document based on information from your SJB states exactly the opposite in black and white, that Captain Dragan -- the military authorities have allowed Captain Dragan to form his training centre in Divic. That's what you and other SJB officials told these republican MUP inspectors when they visited; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where does it say that Vasilic told that to Andan?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, this report also states that: "Due to this decision and the legalisation of the stay by criminally inclined persons, the chief of the SJB has submitted a request to be released from his duty." Now this, late May/early June, the time of this inspection, that was right around the time that Milos Pantelic resigned as SJB chief and you took over; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And at the beginning of the second paragraph I read out to you that the report states that the paramilitaries had committed a number of crimes, even killing Muslim nationals who were ready for exchange. So it appears that you and other SJB officials were well aware that these paramilitary groups were killing Muslims and you reported this to the republican MUP authorities at the time of this inspection in late May or early June; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't know who Mr. Andan talked to and this gentleman who was with him, but I explained this to you a moment ago about the killings in Karakaj and Celopek. As for individual murders in town, they did happen but I don't know who was involved. Was it committed by Zuco's group, Captain Dragan's group, was it the White Eagles group? These corpses that were found, there were Serbs who were killed too, it wasn't only Muslims. I asked for an investigation team to go out on the scene along with an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, whether you knew precisely who the perpetrators were, it's clear from this report you were either the number one or the number two Zvornik police official at the time. You must have known based on this report that paramilitaries were -- had been killing Muslim nationals; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: In town, the town of Zvornik, there was no one else who could have killed Muslims and Serbs - you have to add that too - apart from paramilitaries. I've said this to you very nicely. While I was there, I insisted that teams be set up and that on-site investigations be carried out, and also that these cases should be resolved as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement at paragraphs 40 and 41 you state that in mid-July 1992, you and Branko Grujic secretly went to Pale to inform the leadership about the situation in Zvornik and seek help. You state that you did not personally speak with Dr. Karadzic but that Grujic told you that President Karadzic was visibly surprised by the situation in Zvornik and promised to send a police force to Zvornik. Now, in the Grujic case you testified that this trip to Pale with Mr. Grujic took place sometime in June 1992, not July. And that's right, isn't it, this trip took place in June?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Oh, don't, I'm not sure whether it's June or July. The important thing is that we went to see him, and, quite simply, I did not sleep, I hadn't slept for a long time, and I fell asleep when I was waiting to be seen by Karadzic and I slept through Brano Grujic's meeting and then he told me what he heard from Karadzic. And please don't take my word for this, whether it's June or July, I might have said -- I don't know. But I'm telling you all of this quite frankly, quite sincerely. I mean, I'm not a person who keeps his mouth shut.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note that I'm nearing the end of my time. I think I need about ten more minutes to conclude if that would be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're past your time, but please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vasilic, you said you weren't sure whether it was June or July. I'm going to put to you that it would have made no sense for you and Mr. Grujic to go to Pale to see Dr. Karadzic in mid-July because, in fact, Dr. Karadzic came to Zvornik with General Mladic and met with the Zvornik authorities, including both you and Mr. Grujic, on the 30th of June. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I know that he came, but the date, the month, I didn't give that any thought. I know that Mr. Karadzic came and that Mr. Mladic came.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have P1478, page 246 of the English and 244 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: While we're waiting, wouldn't it be a good thing to ask him whether the meeting in Pale was before or after Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic came? That might help you find if it's in June or July since we know the date of that meeting with Mladic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, that's why I put to him that it couldn't have been July because that wouldn't have made any sense given the presence of the accused in Zvornik on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, this meeting took place on the 30th of June and you were present at it; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is an extract from General Mladic's military notebook recording the conversation at that meeting. And I'd like to go through some of the comments in it with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 250 of the English and 248 of the B/C/S, this --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see whether the name of this witness is mentioned at all or whether we have a completely different Vasilic under number 16?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He's confirmed his presence at this meeting and I will come to his name, and that's an inappropriate intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, this is Mr. Grujic speaking. And you can see around the middle of the page after he says that Marko Pavlovic accomplished much until the formation of the brigade. He says: "In addition to major accomplishments, we also had many problems from various formations, and Dencic called together these groups 'called Zuca and similar,' Captain Dragan appeared out of nowhere requesting to form a centre in Divic ..." That reference to Dencic, that's a reference to Nikola Dencic, the Eastern Bosnia Corps commander; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's the same meeting, whether this Dencic is there or not. I don't know. There is a reference to Vasilic, there was a brigade commander, a certain Vasilic. Just tell me where the meeting was held. If it was held at the municipality, that's the one that I attended. If it was at another location, then I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, right now I'm just asking you whether Mr. Grujic's reference to Dencic calling together groups such as Zuca is a reference to Nikola Dencic, the Eastern Bosnian Corps commander. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't know the gentleman, Mr. Dencic, I never met him personally.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat the last part of his sentence in terms of that person's face.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You've been asked to repeat the last part of your sentence in terms of that person's face. Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Dencic and I could not recognise him by his face anywhere because I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Grujic says: "Captain Dragan appeared out of nowhere requesting to form a centre in Divic ..." That's a reference to Captain Dragan's training centre in Divic; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, then it's not the meeting that I attended. At that meeting where I attended, General Mladic ordered that within 24 hours he should not see Captain Dragan in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's find out whether --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Whether witness is present or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm going to do. Could we go to page 271 of the English, page 269 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I know whether this is the same meeting because there is a considerable difference between pages 244 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are coming to it. I find it's page 246 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Page 271 of the English, page 269 of the B/C/S states: "Chief MUP Marinko Vasilic."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's you, right, Mr. Vasilic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's show him the place of meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't believe the place is identified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It just says: "Meeting with representatives of Zvornik municipality in Zvornik." And -- but the notes are continuous, there are no new entries for these several pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But his name does not appear in the --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It doesn't appear as a -- in the list of attendees, but the notes are continuous without a new heading until page 271 when this witness is recorded as speaking. So from the notes it appears clear that the witness was, in fact, present and spoke although he wasn't listed as an attendee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you put it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I did and he initially confirmed it. I can put it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, do you recall now, can you confirm again that you attended this meeting with Dr. Karadzic, General Mladic, and other members of the Zvornik leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, could the date be specified? I do not believe that Mladic could have made 20 or 30 pages of notes at a single meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll go -- we can skim through the pages. Let's show him the first page first, that's 29th of September, 20 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 30th of June, 1992, page 246 of the English, 244 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, this is 30th of June, 1992, in Zvornik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, wait till we have B/C/S version. Do you have the page number, Ms. Gustafson? Yes, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And there is a list of those present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And then we continue from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Would Your Honour like me to ask a question now or I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, you can see a list of people present. You are not listed here, although later in these notes you are listed as making comments. Can you confirm that you were present at this meeting on the 30th of June, 1992, in Zvornik, with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: What can I say? I can say that I don't know when this happened, but there was this meeting on the premises of the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik that was attended by Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic and some other military personnel. There was no mention of setting up a centre, a training centre, that Captain Dragan had asked for. Among other things, General Mladic explicitly insisted that Captain Dragan -- because, actually, I was the one who conveyed this to him at that meeting. I presented the problems that were involved, and I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please repeat the last part of his sentence because it was unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat from "I presented the problems that were involved ..." And speak very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary, I can repeat my entire thought. I was at this meeting at the Municipal Assembly of Zvornik that was attended by President Radovan Karadzic, General Ratko Mladic, and a number of other persons who I do not know. There were no requests of Captain Dragan's for setting up a training centre. That did not happen there, but I know that General Ratko Mladic insisted that Captain Dragan leave the area of Zvornik within 24 hours, and that is what happened. He took the Vidikovac hotel in Divic on his own and he got people together and started training them, painted some paint on their faces, and these uniforms that they wore, it would really frighten anyone. How could anyone be happy to have them there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Was Captain Dragan also present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because he insisted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vasilic, there were a number of complaints by the Zvornik municipal authorities, such as Mr. Grujic and Mr. Mijatovic, about Captain Dragan and his training centre at this meeting; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Jovo Mijatovic was present. Branko Grujic was certainly present. We all complained about the presence and behaviour of these persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, if we could go to page 270 of the English, page 268 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is Dr. Karadzic speaking and he says: "It would be a shame to abolish the centre. It would be easiest for us to put the incident behind us. The men at the centre are not like Zuca and Crni." Now, first, the centre he's referring to is Captain Dragan's training centre; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I suppose so, I think so, but I do not remember all the things that Mr. Karadzic said or Mr. Mladic said. They were there at that meeting for half an hour, an hour, more than that. But I know, quite simply, that Mladic insisted that this person leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And then he says that the men at the training centre are not like Zuca and Crni, so it's clear he is generally familiar with Zuca and Crni. And in your statement you said that you and Mr. Grujic went to Pale in July to report problems by paramilitaries and that Grujic told you that President Karadzic was visibly surprised by the situation in Zvornik. Now, that evidence doesn't fit with this contemporaneous record from the 30th of June, which indicates that Dr. Karadzic was in Zvornik on the 30th of June and was familiar with the paramilitary issues in Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Karadzic knew Captain Dragan. Maybe he did, maybe he didn't, I don't know. And whether he knew of Zuca or whether he heard from someone else about Zuca or some Crni, I don't know, and I don't know about his comments like that. But all members of paramilitary units, no exception whatsoever, were an evil that came to the territory of the municipality of Zvornik. I don't know of Captain Dragan being any better than they are. Maybe he is, but I don't know and I do not have that impression. Well, maybe he as a person but -- well, you know, you will allow me to say when they paint themselves with all that paint, it's like in Vietnam, and then imagine them with rifles too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 271 of the English, page 269 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And again, Mr. Vasilic, this is -- we saw this a few moments ago. This is where you speak and your comments are recorded by General Mladic. On this page you talk about your personnel levels. And if we could go to the next page, you state that: "Security conditions are at a satisfactory level." And your last comment is: "I am very concerned by nicknames. We have no idea who they are or what they are doing." Mr. Vasilic, in your statement and in your evidence today, you -- I believe in your evidence today you said that the police were almost held prisoner by paramilitaries, they -- in your statement you say that the police ran away from the paramilitaries in fear of their lives and the paramilitaries were the absolute power in the town. Now, that evidence does not square with your comments when the supreme commander and the chief of the Main Staff come to your municipality and you tell them that security conditions are at a satisfactory level, and the only mention you make of paramilitaries is that you are concerned by nicknames because you don't know who they are or what they're doing. That's right, you're greatly exaggerating in your evidence the power the paramilitaries had in Zvornik at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: No, no, no way. That certainly could not have come out of my mouth, that the state of security at the level of the town and municipality is satisfactory. It's not only that it wasn't satisfactory. It was no good at all. Nothing could have been done properly, nothing whatsoever. You could not even carry out an on-site investigation for a traffic accident, let alone robberies and things like that. There were 20 armed men that would crop up immediately. There would be one or two policemen on the road, whereas they would have 20 armed men. They would stand on the road and then you'd have to wait. Whenever they felt like moving, then they'd move. And we were arrested, mistreated, beaten, and that Topola wanted to execute me and Brano Grujic. When I could not ensure my own safety, how could I ensure the safety of citizens? So Madam Judge and Your Honours, that is why I left the force after 20 years of professional work. I left the police, absolutely. It's not that I left a supervisory job in the police. I left the force all together because I didn't want to have any fingers pointed at me someday.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasilic. I no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. I'll start with the latest. Could we please have page 268 displayed in this same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting, while we're waiting, Mr. Vasilic, the attendees of this course that Captain Dragan organised, where did they come from? Were they locals or had they come from elsewhere too?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Some people were recruited from elsewhere, but also there were some locals too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at what was circled here, where Captain Jokic says: "They come for training with a recommendation from units and documentation." And then please read these four lines. The distinguished Madam Gustafson read this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the rest of what I said on the next page. The next page in Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you continue these two lines, what I said, and then Djokanovic. Could you read that out loud?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read this out from the screen, these first two lines, my final remarks, and then could you read out what Djokanovic said.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't have that here. I have something in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you're not looking at the right screen. It's the one on the left, that's Serbian. You have two texts in front of you on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes, half Serbian, half English, but it's all mixed up. And now here there's this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then I'm going to read it out. After that I said: "We should have courses ..." Although that's not the way I speak, this is incorrect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this is something that was added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you are not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I want someone to read this out so that the witness can see it. Page 160 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no. "Although that's not the way I speak, this is incorrect," that is totally inappropriate comment on your part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't bear that improper language is attributed to me. This is illiterate as it is. It is not verbatim, it is not literal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the recruits are in Bijeljina, correct, you see that?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I can't get my bearings here, it's all mixed up, I can't. I can't accept --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we do away with the English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The top of the page, see?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, read it out.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: "We should have courses. "The recruits are in Bijeljina. "Commissioner Dragan Djokanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Keep on reading. What did Dragan say?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: "Marko, you are going beyond your authority. "Work is done in Divic, there is work and order there, nothing is stolen there."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You can stop here. Marko who? Who is he addressing?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Who is talking to whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When Dr. Dragan Djokanovic refers to Marko, who is it?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
