utterances.text: Marko Pavlovic, commander of the TO staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it possible to have a camp for recruits even without Captain Dragan?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: We couldn't have it down there. Someone from the military leadership ought to have decided on that and to assign professional personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was I in favour of Captain Dragan staying or was I in favour of a training course?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: The way I understood you --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was that a course, training, was needed. Now, as for whether it would be Captain Dragan or someone else, in my understanding was unimportant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I missed you standing. I see your point. That was -- the last part was very leading. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we next have D1436.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since it is not very legible, I'll read out paragraph number 2 so that you can tell us whether it corresponds to the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, this is about Brcko, the Serb public -- this is about Brcko -- no, no. Page 5 then. Page 5, paragraph 3. Page 5, I don't think this is it. Page 5 of this document. It was shown during cross-examination. In the Serbian version a page before or after this one. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was read out is the first sentence. Can you continue? I'll read out and you can follow. "Also, the aforementioned groups threatened with carrying out an attack on the Zvornik Public Security Station because the police employees stood up to their looting and robbing. What is interesting to be mentioned is that the same people held in encirclement the government building and the building of the Crisis Staff of four to five hours with military equipment. One of the paramilitary formations belonging to Captain Dragan's unit threatened the government president holding a gun to his throat." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. These members of paramilitary units came there with their combat vehicles, with three-barrelled guns, and blocked the facilities. It is correct that they threatened with assaulting the police station because the police and local authorities were against their presence there and their conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said, but were not allowed to complete, what you had gone through. Perhaps you can explain briefly. You as the authorities, how did you fare? What sort of things did you have to go through?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much for allowing me to address it. At the outset, I need to say that we were not the authorities, we had no power. Power is something you hold in your hands and then you have it. We were simple detainees, prisoners. We were trying to take shelter from dangers elsewhere and yet we were threatened by our own compatriots. We were kept prisoner, I, Brano Grujic, Marko Pavlovic, Milos Pantelic, and several others were held prisoner for five to six hours in the TO staff. Zuca kicked the door and came in with five or six of his men and put guns to the backs of our head and asked us who we were, what we were doing, who authorised us, accused us of protecting the Muslims and so on and so forth. After that, there is -- there was worse. There was a barricade, a roadblock, in the centre of town. Brano Grujic and I as well as the Glinica director were kicked out at gunpoint. Topola, who towers at over 2 metres, said that he was tasked with executing us. He was leading us somewhere to execute us and people gathered. We begged to be released. We told him, "Do whatever you like, just let us go." And the next day I and Branko Grujic, as the chief of station and the president of municipality -- actually, I resigned. As of that day, I no longer entered the police station. This is the kind of authorities we were. There's more but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 14 -- sorry, 74, line 14, I think, there is mention of Miljanovic whose buses were used to transport prisoners. Could Miljanovic say no? Could he deny the buses?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Miko Miljanovic, who was a policeman, escorted the inhabitants of Divic on a bus to Celopek with the intention of allowing those people to go further afield because at Divic no one could guarantee their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was my mistake. The director of Drinatrans, could he refuse to provide the buses?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I see no way how he could have, no way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the topic of investigation, the investigation of Drinjaca, can you tell us how many policemen did the reserve police station in Drinjaca have and what were their occupations as well as where they hailed from?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: The reserve police station in Drinjaca perhaps had up to ten people we most. There was one active-duty policeman and the rest were locksmiths, carpenters, craftsmen from the nearby villages, honest, decent people who never had an argument with anyone, let alone use weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could they stand up to this Matic and his men?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. Even if they had a greater force. If I was unable to stand up to them, as I am and I'm not afraid of many things and I had more men than I see -- I don't see how they could have done it up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was Lieutenant Matic killed?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: If my information is correct, then it was sometime in June in Vitinice. I'm not stating anything decidedly, but that's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Drinjaca.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: In Drinjaca, in 1992. I don't know what month, perhaps May, early April -- actually, end of April, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 59 you were asked about the TO plus Arkan, i.e., who liberated Zvornik. Tell us this please: When the volunteers came before the VRS was established, who did they report to in the municipality, to the police or the TO?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: The TO. In principle, they had nothing to do with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can explain. As far as I know, while they came individually or in groups of two or three, they were made part of the TO. But when their numbers increased, then they split up and established their own groups. And I dare say that later on they didn't even obey the brigade commander or anyone. No one controlled them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that you saw the excerpt from Mladic's diary where mention is made of Zuca and Crni and of me knowing, can you say whether you and Brano came to see me in June or July? This arrival of ours in Zvornik, does it have anything to do with the situation there?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I can't say anything decidedly, but I'm inclined to say that it was July, although I am not certain. But I think it was July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know why we came there and assembled you? What was the reason of our arrival?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I had not been informed prior to it, but I supposed you were there to learn what was going on, what the situation was, and to gather information. I was there briefly only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you know about the preparation of arrest operation? When did it begin and when did it end?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Upon my departure and when Brano left, perhaps two or three days around the 29th or the 30th of July, I learned, although I wasn't in the police, that strong special forces arrived from the RS MUP and that in co-ordination with the military police they arrested if not all then at least most, around a hundred men, members of the paramilitary forces and that they were taken to Bijeljina to prison. Some were apparently prosecuted in -- before RS courts, others before the courts of the Republic of Serbia. I also know that Mr. Zuco, two months ago, took part in a TV broadcast called "Happy," where he admitted to his brother being mentally ill and under influence and that in that state he committed the crimes in Celopek. Had there not been about -- the arrest, the question is how long would these executions of theirs have lasted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 15 you said he was doped and here we have that he was under the influence.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: He was a drug addict. Then he was asked, "Well, you knew what he was like." And it seems he tried to keep him under control that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly have P6405 or 65 ter 25215. Page 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were shown it today. I'll read out from line 4. Please listen to it. [In English] "That was talked about for about a half of year, and I guess I heard ..." [Interpretation] Does it say here that you know for sure or that you assume so?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question, but I understand what you read out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'll read only that part. [In English] "... and I guess I heard ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do not lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I wanted to ascertain on this page in several places whether he knew or he guessed or he heard or believed so. Well, on page 9 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can read it. "I guess I heard about it," it says.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That was the page, and during cross-examination the question was put to him as if he were certain. And my last question has to do with P2591. P2591. Item III, can we go to the beginning. This is about the establishment of the Serbian municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read item III to us. It isn't long. Please read it out aloud.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: "Decision on the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item III.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: "The local communes, inhabited places, and parts of the local communes of the cities, as by Article 2 of this decision, are being separated from the municipality of Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was there an option of this being implemented by force and include a Muslim settlement in this Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: I replied a number of times that I wasn't involved in politics, but from what I heard and learned by talking to people, I can say that the intention was to talk and try to agree and solve problems in a peaceful manner. If necessary, the municipality can be split into a Serbian part and a Muslim part. I have never heard the war -- war as an option -- being mentioned as an option.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did the Serbs think that Snagovo should be part of their municipality? Why only one Snagovo? Because there are three places called Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: Because that Snagovo has a Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about Snagovo Donje and Snagovo Gornje?

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: These are inhabited by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasilic, for your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MARINKO VASILIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Vasilic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have a long weekend and resume on Wednesday at 9.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
